items.prompt:
A teacher reads:
'Volcanoes form when magma from deep inside the Earth pushes through weak spots in the crust. When magma reaches the surface, it is called lava. Volcanoes can be found on land and on the ocean floor. Some of the Hawaiian Islands were formed by underwater volcanoes.'

A student retells: 'Volcanoes are made of lava and they are hot.' Identify TWO key ideas missing from this retelling.
A) The names of specific volcanoes / how hot lava is
B) How volcanoes form (magma through weak spots in crust) / that some Hawaiian Islands were formed by underwater volcanoes
C) That volcanoes are dangerous / that scientists study volcanoes
items.answer: B) How volcanoes form (magma through weak spots in crust) / that some Hawaiian Islands were formed by underwater volcanoes

steps: The student's retelling only says 'made of lava and hot' — very vague.
Missing key idea 1: HOW volcanoes form — magma pushes through weak spots in Earth's crust.
Missing key idea 2: A specific application — some Hawaiian Islands were formed by underwater volcanoes.
Neither 'specific volcano names' nor 'scientists study volcanoes' were stated in this passage.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads a complex passage about the water cycle with four stages: evaporation, condensation, precipitation, and collection. A student retells only the first two stages. The teacher asks: 'Is this a complete retelling?' The student says: 'I think I got the important parts.' How should the teacher respond?
A) 'Yes, two stages is enough.'
B) 'You covered evaporation and condensation well, but precipitation (water falling as rain or snow) and collection (water gathering in rivers, lakes, and oceans) are also key parts of the cycle that your retelling is missing.'
C) 'Only the first stage matters — start over.'
items.answer: B) 'You covered evaporation and condensation well, but precipitation (water falling as rain or snow) and collection (water gathering in rivers, lakes, and oceans) are also key parts of the cycle that your retelling is missing.'

steps: A complete retelling of a process includes ALL the key stages, not just the first ones.
The water cycle has four stages; omitting two leaves the picture incomplete.
The teacher's response validates what was correct (first two stages) while identifying what is missing.
This is the correct coaching approach: acknowledge + identify gaps.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads a story about a girl named Lena who wanted to enter a science fair. She was nervous but built a model volcano, practiced her presentation 10 times, and won third place. Afterward, her teacher asked: 'What information did you gather about how Lena prepared?' A student answers: 'She worked hard.' Is this enough? What specific information is missing?
A) This is enough — 'worked hard' is the key idea
B) Not enough — the specific preparation steps are the key information: she built a model volcano and practiced her presentation 10 times
C) This is too much — only the result (winning) matters
items.answer: B) Not enough — the specific preparation steps are the key information: she built a model volcano and practiced her presentation 10 times

steps: The teacher asked specifically about HOW Lena prepared — a detail question.
'She worked hard' is a vague summary that doesn't use any specific details from the passage.
The key information: she built a model volcano (what she made) and practiced 10 times (how many times).
Specific details demonstrate that the student was listening carefully to the read-aloud.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads a passage about the moon landings:
'In 1969, astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the moon. He was part of the Apollo 11 mission. Armstrong said his famous words: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind." The mission also included astronaut Buzz Aldrin.'

A student retells: 'Neil Armstrong walked on the moon in 1969 and said something famous.' What two improvements would make this retelling more complete?
A) Add the exact quote AND mention the mission name (Apollo 11) and Buzz Aldrin
B) Add the country that sent them AND the rocket's weight
C) Add what Armstrong ate for breakfast AND the weather that day
items.answer: A) Add the exact quote AND mention the mission name (Apollo 11) and Buzz Aldrin

steps: Improvement 1: The student says Armstrong 'said something famous' but doesn't include the quote. The exact words — 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind' — are a key detail.
Improvement 2: The mission name (Apollo 11) and Buzz Aldrin were both mentioned in the passage and are notable details.
Country and rocket weight were not in the passage; breakfast and weather are irrelevant.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads an article that presents two points of view about screen time: one expert says screens harm children's development, another says educational screens are beneficial. A student retells only the first view. What is the problem?
A) There is no problem — one view is enough
B) The retelling is incomplete because the passage presented BOTH views; leaving out the second view gives a one-sided summary
C) The student should have retold neither view
items.answer: B) The retelling is incomplete because the passage presented BOTH views; leaving out the second view gives a one-sided summary

steps: When a passage presents multiple perspectives, a complete retelling includes all of them.
Leaving out the second view misrepresents the passage as one-sided.
The student should note: 'One expert said screens are harmful, while another said educational screens can be helpful.'
Listening carefully means capturing all the key ideas — even ones you might not agree with.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads a story where the sequence of events matters: (1) a seed is planted, (2) it rains, (3) the seed sprouts, (4) the plant grows a flower, (5) bees pollinate the flower, (6) a new seed forms. A student retells events 1, 3, and 6 but skips 2, 4, and 5. Why does this matter?
A) It doesn't — three events are enough
B) The skipped steps (rain, flower growth, pollination) explain HOW each event caused the next; without them, the retelling loses the causal chain
C) Events 4 and 5 are not important
items.answer: B) The skipped steps (rain, flower growth, pollination) explain HOW each event caused the next; without them, the retelling loses the causal chain

steps: In a sequence of events, each step causes or enables the next.
Skipping 'it rains' leaves out WHY the seed sprouted.
Skipping 'flower grows' leaves out WHY bees could pollinate.
Skipping 'bees pollinate' leaves out HOW the new seed formed.
A complete retelling of a sequence must preserve the causal chain.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads an informational passage about sharks. Afterward, she asks three different questions:
  Q1: 'What is the main idea of this passage?'
  Q2: 'What do sharks eat?'
  Q3: 'What did you learn about how sharks hunt?'
Explain what type of listening response each question is asking for.
A) Q1: key idea / Q2: specific detail / Q3: specific detail about a process
B) Q1: personal opinion / Q2: key idea / Q3: personal connection
C) All three questions ask for the same type of response
items.answer: A) Q1: key idea / Q2: specific detail / Q3: specific detail about a process

steps: Q1 asks for the MAIN IDEA — the overall point of the whole passage.
Q2 asks for a SPECIFIC DETAIL — a particular fact stated in the text (what sharks eat).
Q3 asks for a SPECIFIC DETAIL ABOUT A PROCESS — how sharks hunt; this requires recounting steps or methods.
Recognizing what type of response is needed helps you give the right kind of retelling.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads a complex passage about ancient Rome with these key ideas:
(1) Rome was one of the greatest empires in history.
(2) Romans built roads, aqueducts, and famous buildings like the Colosseum.
(3) Latin, the language of Rome, is the root of many modern languages.
(4) The Roman Empire fell in 476 AD.

A student retells: 'Ancient Rome was a great empire. They built roads and buildings.' Evaluate this retelling: what is done well and what key ideas are missing?
A) Well: captures (1) and part of (2). Missing: aqueducts from (2), Latin/languages (3), and the fall of Rome (4)
B) Well: nothing. Missing: everything in the passage
C) This is a complete retelling — no key ideas are missing
items.answer: A) Well: captures (1) and part of (2). Missing: aqueducts from (2), Latin/languages (3), and the fall of Rome (4)

steps: The student correctly identified that Rome was great (point 1) and mentioned roads and buildings (part of point 2).
Missing from point 2: aqueducts were also mentioned alongside roads and buildings.
Missing entirely: point 3 (Latin as the root of modern languages) — a key and distinctive fact.
Missing entirely: point 4 (the Roman Empire fell in 476 AD) — a key historical conclusion.
A strong retelling would include all four key ideas.

items.prompt:
After a read-aloud, a teacher asks: 'What was the author's most important message in this passage about ocean pollution?' A student answers: 'Oceans are getting polluted.' Another student says: 'The author's most important message is that plastic pollution is the biggest threat to ocean life, and everyone — governments, businesses, and people — needs to act now to stop it.' Which response better answers the question?
A) The first — shorter answers are always stronger
B) The second — it identifies the specific type of pollution (plastic), the specific concern (threat to ocean life), and the author's call to action (everyone must act)
C) Both responses are equally strong
items.answer: B) The second — it identifies the specific type of pollution (plastic), the specific concern (threat to ocean life), and the author's call to action (everyone must act)

steps: The first response is too vague — it does not identify the specific message.
The second response captures three specific elements: type (plastic), impact (threat to ocean life), and message (everyone must act).
The question asks for the 'most important message' — this requires identifying what the AUTHOR wanted the reader to understand and do.
Specificity is the mark of careful listening.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads a passage, and a student retells it accurately. The teacher then asks: 'What was one piece of information you gathered that surprised you or that you did not know before?' A student answers: 'I didn't know that honey never expires — archaeologists found 3,000-year-old honey in Egyptian tombs and it was still edible.' Is this an appropriate response?
A) No — surprises and personal reactions are never part of gathering information
B) Yes — the student is connecting personal prior knowledge (what they did NOT know) to a specific new detail from the read-aloud
C) No — only the most important facts count as gathered information
items.answer: B) Yes — the student is connecting personal prior knowledge (what they did NOT know) to a specific new detail from the read-aloud

steps: The standard says: describe key ideas or details from a text read aloud or information presented orally.
The student correctly identifies a specific detail from the passage (honey never expires, 3,000-year-old honey found in Egyptian tombs).
Noting what was new to them is a reflection on LEARNING, which deepens engagement with the text.
This is a strong, appropriate response — personal connection PLUS specific text detail.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads a story with a theme about perseverance. The events are: (1) a girl tries to learn to ride a bike, (2) she falls many times, (3) she keeps trying, (4) she finally rides successfully. A student retells: 'A girl learned to ride a bike.' Identify the missing elements and explain why they matter.
A) Missing: the struggles (falling) and the persistence (kept trying) — these events show the theme of perseverance, which is the point of the story
B) Missing: the type of bike and the location
C) Nothing is missing — the retelling is complete
items.answer: A) Missing: the struggles (falling) and the persistence (kept trying) — these events show the theme of perseverance, which is the point of the story

steps: The retelling ('a girl learned to ride a bike') captures only the beginning and end.
Events 2 and 3 (falling, kept trying) are the heart of the story — they show perseverance.
Without those events, the story's theme is lost.
In a story where the theme matters, the key events that BUILD to the resolution are the key details.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads an informational text about the rain forest canopy. The passage explains: (1) the canopy is the top layer of trees, (2) it blocks most sunlight, (3) most rain forest animals live in the canopy, (4) canopy animals include monkeys, sloths, and parrots. A student retells: 'The canopy is the top layer. Animals live there.' What is missing, and does it matter?
A) The specific animal examples and the function of the canopy (blocking sunlight) are missing; they matter because they are specific details the passage emphasized
B) Nothing is missing — top layer and animals are the key ideas
C) The missing part is the type of rain forest
items.answer: A) The specific animal examples and the function of the canopy (blocking sunlight) are missing; they matter because they are specific details the passage emphasized

steps: The retelling correctly identifies that the canopy is the top layer and that animals live there.
Missing: the canopy's function — it blocks most sunlight. This is why lower layers are dim.
Missing: specific animal examples — monkeys, sloths, and parrots. Specific examples strengthen a retelling.
Details that explain HOW or WHY (blocking sunlight) and specific examples (animal names) demonstrate careful listening.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads a passage presenting a cause-and-effect relationship: 'When forests are cut down, animals lose their homes. Without homes, populations of birds, mammals, and insects decline. As insect populations drop, plants that depend on pollination also suffer.' A student retells: 'Cutting down forests is bad.' What makes this retelling inadequate for a Grade 2 listener?
A) The student expressed an opinion instead of explaining the cause-and-effect chain stated in the passage
B) The student should not have expressed any view about forests
C) The retelling is adequate — opinions are fine
items.answer: A) The student expressed an opinion instead of explaining the cause-and-effect chain stated in the passage

steps: 'Cutting down forests is bad' is a vague opinion, not a retelling of the cause-and-effect chain.
The passage described a specific chain: cutting forests (cause) → animals lose homes → populations decline → pollination-dependent plants suffer.
A strong retelling would explain each link in the chain.
Retellings should describe what the text said, not just whether the student agrees with it.

items.prompt:
A teacher reads two passages about the same topic (ancient Egypt) on two different days. On day 2, a student incorporates details from both readings into their retelling. Is this appropriate?
A) No — each retelling should only reference the most recent reading
B) Yes — combining information from multiple related texts to build a fuller picture is a strong listening comprehension skill
C) No — comparing texts is only allowed in reading class
items.answer: B) Yes — combining information from multiple related texts to build a fuller picture is a strong listening comprehension skill

steps: The standard says: recount or describe key ideas from a text read aloud OR information presented through other media.
Using information from related texts shows the student is making connections across presentations.
This is a strength — it demonstrates that the student retained information from the first reading and integrated new information from the second.
Building a fuller picture from multiple sources is an important comprehension skill.

items.prompt:
After a read-aloud, a teacher says: 'I noticed that when I retell, I try to explain not just WHAT happened but WHY it happened. Can you try that with the passage we just heard?' A student retells: 'The passage said that bats sleep during the day BECAUSE they hunt at night, and they hunt at night BECAUSE their special hearing called echolocation works better in the dark.' Evaluate this retelling.
A) Weak — the student should just list facts without explaining reasons
B) Strong — the student used cause-and-effect language ('because') to explain both what happened and why
C) Incomplete — the student only mentioned echolocation
items.answer: B) Strong — the student used cause-and-effect language ('because') to explain both what happened and why

steps: The teacher specifically asked for WHAT and WHY — cause and effect.
The student used 'because' twice to link causes to effects: sleep during day because hunt at night; hunt at night because echolocation works better in dark.
This retelling goes beyond listing facts to explaining relationships — a sophisticated listening response.
Echolocation WAS mentioned and explained — that is not missing, it is the key explanation.
